variants.title: Follow one prediction
variants.context: One prediction runs from prompt to response: tokenize the request, build a logit for every possible next token from the retained context, turn those scores into probabilities with softmax, then decode a token and append it before repeating. Each output token becomes part of the next input.
variants.prompt: A user sends a short question to a chat endpoint. Put the steps that produce the first output token in order.

items.text: Transformer layers combine the retained tokens into a logit for every possible next token.
Softmax converts the logits into a probability distribution over candidates.
The decoder picks a token from the allowed set and appends it before the cycle repeats.
Tokenization maps the request text to vocabulary IDs the model can operate on.

variants.hint: Which representation does the model actually compute on?
variants.explanation: Scores come before probabilities and probabilities come before a choice, so decoding settings act last on evidence that is already fixed.

variants.title: Follow one prediction
variants.context: One prediction runs from prompt to response: tokenize the request, build a logit for every possible next token from the retained context, turn those scores into probabilities with softmax, then decode a token and append it before repeating. Each output token becomes part of the next input.
variants.prompt: An operator raises temperature from 0.2 to 1.1 and the answer changes. Put the steps in order to show where that setting acts.

items.text: Temperature rescales those logits before softmax, flattening the distribution.
The layers produce the same logits they would produce at any temperature.
Sampling draws from the widened allowed set, so a lower-ranked continuation can be emitted.
The prompt and retrieved excerpts are tokenized into the context window.

variants.hint: Does the setting change the evidence or only the selection?
variants.explanation: Temperature changes how concentrated the distribution is, so it changes which supported continuation is emitted and adds no new evidence.

variants.title: Follow one prediction
variants.context: One prediction runs from prompt to response: tokenize the request, build a logit for every possible next token from the retained context, turn those scores into probabilities with softmax, then decode a token and append it before repeating. Each output token becomes part of the next input.
variants.prompt: A retrieval-backed answer goes wrong at its second sentence. Put the steps in order to show how one early choice propagates.

items.text: Every later token is scored under the path the earlier choice created.
The first output token is decoded from the candidate distribution.
That token is appended to the input, changing the condition for the next score.
The assembled prompt and sources are encoded into the context window.

variants.hint: What is different about the input on the second step?
variants.explanation: Each output token becomes part of the next input, so an early decoding choice can send the whole response down a different path.

variants.title: Stage the training work
variants.context: Behavior is trained in stages: pre-training learns a language prior from broad next-token prediction, post-training shapes task behavior from demonstrations and preferences, evaluation measures quality and failure slices, and operation adds versioning, tracing, and rollback.
variants.prompt: A team is planning the work that produces a shippable assistant. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Operate with versioned prompts and models, traced retrieval and tool calls, and a rollback path.
Post-train with demonstrations and preference data to improve instruction following and format control.
Pre-train on broad data by predicting the next token to build a language prior.
Evaluate task quality, calibration, safety, factuality, and failure slices on held-out data.

variants.hint: Which stage teaches patterns, and which one teaches behavior?
variants.explanation: Training creates general tendencies, but the runtime evidence and safety system is a separate stage that training does not replace.

variants.title: Stage the training work
variants.context: Behavior is trained in stages: pre-training learns a language prior from broad next-token prediction, post-training shapes task behavior from demonstrations and preferences, evaluation measures quality and failure slices, and operation adds versioning, tracing, and rollback.
variants.prompt: A model follows instructions well but cites stale facts. Put the stages in order and note where the fix belongs.

items.text: Operation adds retrieval configuration, traces, and a rollback path so the fix can be released and reversed.
Evaluation measures factuality on held-out prompts and isolates the stale-fact slice.
Pre-training gave the model its language prior, which does not guarantee that a fact is current.
Post-training improved instruction following, which is why the formatting already looks correct.

variants.hint: Which stage can actually supply a current fact?
variants.explanation: Post-training shapes behavior rather than knowledge, so a freshness failure is answered by the runtime evidence path, not by more instruction tuning.

variants.title: Stage the training work
variants.context: Behavior is trained in stages: pre-training learns a language prior from broad next-token prediction, post-training shapes task behavior from demonstrations and preferences, evaluation measures quality and failure slices, and operation adds versioning, tracing, and rollback.
variants.prompt: A new quantized build is ready. Put the stages in order for the release path that build has to travel.

items.text: Evaluation compares output quality, tool-call formats, safety behavior, and long-context retrieval against the previous build.
Post-training artifacts such as prompt templates and tool formats are pinned to the build.
The pre-trained prior is unchanged by the numerics work.
Operation records the release, ships a canary, and keeps rollback available if quality or cost regresses.

variants.hint: A smaller footprint is not a release decision by itself.
variants.explanation: Numerics changes need versioned offline slices and staged telemetry, because behavior can shift without any visible error.

variants.title: Size the weight footprint
variants.context: Weight memory is the parameter count multiplied by the bytes each parameter occupies: two bytes under BF16 and one byte under FP8 or INT8. Sparse activation can cut compute per token, but it does not make the inactive weights free to store.
variants.prompt: A dense model has 32 billion parameters and is served with BF16 weights, which use two bytes per parameter. How much weight memory does one worker need?
variants.hint: Multiply the parameter count by the bytes each parameter occupies.
variants.explanation: Weight memory is parameters times bytes per parameter, which is why precision is a capacity decision before it is a quality decision.

mistakes.feedback: That uses one byte per parameter, which is the FP8 or INT8 assumption rather than BF16.
That uses four bytes per parameter, which is FP32 and not the precision described.

variants.title: Size the weight footprint
variants.context: Weight memory is the parameter count multiplied by the bytes each parameter occupies: two bytes under BF16 and one byte under FP8 or INT8. Sparse activation can cut compute per token, but it does not make the inactive weights free to store.
variants.prompt: A dense model has 70 billion parameters and a team moves it to FP8 weights at one byte per parameter. How much weight memory do the weights need?
variants.hint: Change only the bytes per parameter, not the parameter count.
variants.explanation: Lower-precision weights reduce the weight footprint proportionally, but the KV cache usually stays at higher precision and does not shrink with them.

mistakes.feedback: That keeps two bytes per parameter, which is the BF16 footprint before the change.
That halves the FP8 result again, applying the precision reduction twice.

variants.title: Size the weight footprint
variants.context: Weight memory is the parameter count multiplied by the bytes each parameter occupies: two bytes under BF16 and one byte under FP8 or INT8. Sparse activation can cut compute per token, but it does not make the inactive weights free to store.
variants.prompt: An MoE model stores 64 billion parameters across 8 equal experts and routes each token through 2 of them. Weights are BF16 at two bytes per parameter. How much weight memory must the worker hold?
variants.hint: Routing decides what runs, not what has to be resident.
variants.explanation: Sparse activation reduces compute per token, but every expert weight must still be stored, moved, and operated.

mistakes.feedback: That counts only the two active experts, which is the active compute path and not the stored footprint.
That uses one byte per parameter instead of the two bytes BF16 requires.

variants.title: Name the production failure
variants.context: Production LLM systems fail in named ways: context eviction drops the decisive source, a confident unsupported answer has no evidence behind it, KV-cache exhaustion runs out of memory before the weights do, MoE imbalance concentrates tokens on a few experts, and an optimization can silently change behavior.
variants.prompt: A long document is summarized correctly at 4,000 tokens of input but misses a clause when the same document arrives with three extra sources attached. What is the leading failure?
options: Context eviction, because the decisive excerpt fell outside the window.
KV-cache exhaustion, because concurrent sequences ran the worker out of memory.
A silent regression, because a decoder default changed between the two runs.
optionFeedback: Correct, adding sources pushed the needed text past the budget, and text outside the window cannot affect the next token.
Cache exhaustion fails the request or queues it, rather than quietly returning a summary missing one clause.
Nothing changed between the runs except the input length, so a version change is not the explanation.
variants.hint: What is different between the two requests?
variants.explanation: Text outside the context window cannot influence the calculation, so test with required evidence placed near the budget boundary.

variants.title: Name the production failure
variants.context: Production LLM systems fail in named ways: context eviction drops the decisive source, a confident unsupported answer has no evidence behind it, KV-cache exhaustion runs out of memory before the weights do, MoE imbalance concentrates tokens on a few experts, and an optimization can silently change behavior.
variants.prompt: Time to first token climbs sharply at peak hours, requests are rejected while weight memory is unchanged, and average prompt length has doubled this month. What should the team investigate first?
options: KV-cache pressure from long prompts and concurrent sequences.
Expert routing skew that is overloading a small set of experts.
A confident unsupported output path that lacks a verifier.
optionFeedback: Correct, long prompts and many concurrent sequences exhaust cache memory before weight storage becomes the limit.
Routing skew applies to MoE serving and would show as per-expert hotspots, not as growth tied to prompt length.
An unsupported answer is a quality failure and does not explain queueing and rejections.
variants.hint: Which memory grows with sequence length rather than with model size?
variants.explanation: Enforce per-request budgets, admission control, and queue limits, because the cache can exhaust memory long before the weights do.

variants.title: Name the production failure
variants.context: Production LLM systems fail in named ways: context eviction drops the decisive source, a confident unsupported answer has no evidence behind it, KV-cache exhaustion runs out of memory before the weights do, MoE imbalance concentrates tokens on a few experts, and an optimization can silently change behavior.
variants.prompt: A model answers a policy question fluently and with high probability on every token, but the cited regulation does not exist. What does that tell the team?
options: The context window was too small, so the answer should be retried with more tokens.
A high-probability continuation is not evidence, so this claim needed a verifier.
The decoding temperature was too high, so the sampler picked an unsupported path.
optionFeedback: A larger window helps only when the missing evidence exists and was truncated, which is not established here.
Correct, probability is conditional on context and parameters, so consequential claims need citation checks or tool verification.
Lower temperature would make the same unsupported continuation more likely, not less.
variants.hint: What exactly does a high token probability establish?
variants.explanation: A high-probability token is the model's best continuation under its context, not proof that the token is true.

variants.title: Watch the signal that catches the failure
variants.context: Each named failure has a signal that detects it. Monitoring is only useful when the signal you watch matches the risk you actually carry.
variants.prompt: Match each production failure to the signal that most directly detects it.

pairs.label: Silent regression

variants.explanation: Monitoring is only useful when each watched signal corresponds to a specific risk the system actually carries.

variants.prompt: A release record is being written. Match each monitoring group to the question it answers.

pairs.label: Answer quality
pairs.detail: Task success, grounded-claim rate, citation validity, and abstention appropriateness

pairs.label: Safety and security
pairs.detail: Policy violations, prompt-injection success, and tool authorization failures

pairs.label: Serving health
pairs.detail: Time to first token, tokens per second, queue wait, and cancellation rate

pairs.label: Cost and change control
pairs.detail: Tokens per successful task, cache hit rate, and rollback time

variants.hint: Group the metrics by the decision they inform, not by where they are emitted.
variants.explanation: A release record ties model version, prompt template, retrieval configuration, decoding defaults, and evidence together so each risk has an owner.

variants.title: Watch the signal that catches the failure
variants.context: Each named failure has a signal that detects it. Monitoring is only useful when the signal you watch matches the risk you actually carry.
variants.prompt: Match each part of the evidence path to the job it performs for a factual answer.

pairs.label: Retrieve
pairs.detail: Fetch current permissioned sources and rank them, which bounds what the answer can ground in

pairs.label: Fit
pairs.detail: Reserve tokens for instructions, excerpts, tool output, and the answer within the window

pairs.label: Verify
pairs.detail: Check citations, run authoritative tools, or route the uncertain case to review

pairs.label: Abstain
pairs.detail: Say the evidence is missing, ask a focused follow-up, or offer a cited alternative

variants.hint: Which stage sets the ceiling on everything after it?
variants.explanation: Retrieval quality bounds what the model can ground in, and abstention needs product support or the system will force a completion instead.
